title: Hidden gems
headline: The Italy most visitors drive straight past
tagline: Hill villages, small islands, quiet coasts and handsome cities where you can still get a table without booking and hear more Italian than English.

hero_image.alt: Civita di Bagnoregio on its tufa pinnacle above the badlands, joined to the world by a long footbridge
hero_image.credit: Esniom, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

intro: Italy's famous places are famous for good reason, but they are a small slice of the country. Step one valley, one ferry or one train stop beyond the headline names and the pace changes: the bar owner remembers your order on day two, the lane to the church is empty at ten in the morning, and dinner costs what locals pay. None of the places below is a secret, exactly. They are simply loved mostly by Italians.

We have grouped them by mood rather than by region, and each card tells you why it is worth the detour and when it is at its best. Two quality marks are useful for finding more: I Borghi più Belli d'Italia, a club of more than 350 small historic villages, and the Touring Club Italiano's Bandiere Arancioni (orange flags), held by around 300 small inland towns for hospitality, heritage and care of the landscape.

sections.heading: Villages that time forgot
sections.intro: Stone villages on ridges and cliffs, some lovingly restored, one entirely abandoned. Stay the night if you can: they come alive when the day visitors leave.

items.title: Civita di Bagnoregio
items.subtitle: Lazio, between Orvieto and Lake Bolsena
items.desc: A medieval village on a pinnacle of crumbling tufa, reached only by a long, steep footbridge across the badlands of the Valle dei Calanchi. A handful of people still live here. There is a small entry fee; pay it, then linger in the lanes, the cellar wine bars and the belvedere over the clay gullies.
items.meta: Why: a town on a vanishing rock · When: early morning, or misty October days

image.alt: The medieval houses of Civita di Bagnoregio seen from the pedestrian bridge, above eroded cliffs
image.credit: Einaz80, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Santo Stefano di Sessanio
items.subtitle: Abruzzo, Gran Sasso National Park
items.desc: A fortified shepherds' village at about 1,250 metres, built by the wool trade and rescued from abandonment by careful restoration. Eat the tiny local lentils, walk up to the hilltop castle of Rocca Calascio, and drive across the vast Campo Imperatore plateau, nicknamed Italy's little Tibet.
items.meta: Why: mountain silence and wool-trade stone · When: June to October

image.alt: A sunny cobbled lane between stone houses in Santo Stefano di Sessanio
image.credit: Marica Massaro, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Craco
items.subtitle: Basilicata, an hour from Matera
items.desc: A hilltop town emptied by landslides in the 1960s and left exactly as it was, its towers and palazzi slowly settling into the clay. You can visit only on a guided tour with a helmet, which makes it feel even more haunting. Film crews love it; you will see why.
items.meta: Why: Italy's most striking ghost town · When: spring or autumn, late afternoon light

image.alt: Aerial view of the abandoned hilltop town of Craco among clay hills
image.credit: Maurizio Moro5153, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Bosa
items.subtitle: Sardinia, west coast
items.desc: A sweep of pastel houses climbing from the River Temo to the Malaspina castle, with old tanneries along the water and a beach at Bosa Marina. Taste the amber Malvasia di Bosa, then drive the cliff road north towards Alghero, one of the island's loveliest.
items.meta: Why: colour, river life and sweet Malvasia · When: May to June, September

image.alt: Bosa's pastel houses along the River Temo winding towards the sea
image.credit: Zsuzsanna Tóth, CC0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Castelmezzano
items.subtitle: Basilicata, Lucanian Dolomites
items.desc: Houses wedged between jagged sandstone spires, facing its twin village Pietrapertosa across the valley. Walk the Path of the Seven Stones between them, climb the via ferrata, or, if you dare, fly across on the Volo dell'Angelo, a steel-cable zip line high above the gorge.
items.meta: Why: village-on-the-rocks drama · When: May to September (zip line is seasonal)

image.alt: A rider on the Volo dell'Angelo zip line above Castelmezzano and its sandstone peaks
image.credit: Lorenzo Palazzo, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

sections.heading: Quiet islands
sections.intro: Skip the ferry queue to Capri and try one of these. Most are reached by hydrofoil or ferry in under two hours, and all reward a few nights rather than a day trip.

items.title: Procida
items.subtitle: Campania, Bay of Naples
items.desc: The smallest island in the bay and the least polished, which is the point. Marina Corricella's ice-cream-coloured fishermen's houses, the fortified old town of Terra Murata, lemon gardens and a few small beaches. Ferries and hydrofoils from Naples take 40 to 60 minutes.
items.meta: Why: real island life near Naples · When: May to June, September to October

image.alt: Colourful fishermen's houses and boats in the harbour of Marina Corricella, Procida
image.credit: Ekrem Canli, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Favignana
items.subtitle: Sicily, Egadi Islands
items.desc: A flat, butterfly-shaped island made for cycling: rent a bike at the port and pedal between turquoise coves like Cala Rossa and Bue Marino. The vast former Florio tuna cannery is now a superb museum. Hydrofoils from Trapani take about half an hour.
items.meta: Why: bikes, coves and tuna history · When: June, September

image.alt: Turquoise water and rocks at Cala Azzurra on the island of Favignana
image.credit: Ugeorge, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Ustica
items.subtitle: Sicily, north of Palermo
items.desc: A small black volcanic island ringed by Italy's first marine protected area, created in 1986. Divers and snorkellers come for the clear water, grottoes and groupers; everyone else for the coastal path, the lighthouse and grilled fish on the harbour. Boats leave from Palermo.
items.meta: Why: some of Italy's clearest water · When: June to September

image.alt: The harbour and pastel village of Ustica seen from the hill above
image.credit: Miceli vincenzo, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Pantelleria
items.subtitle: Sicily, closer to Tunisia than to Palermo
items.desc: A wild volcanic island of black lava, low-domed stone dammusi, caper bushes and wind-sheltered zibibbo vines, whose head-trained growing method is UNESCO-listed. Bathe in the hot-spring-fed Lago di Venere and drink passito with almond biscuits. Fly from Palermo or Trapani.
items.meta: Why: stark beauty, sweet wine · When: May to June, September to October

image.alt: Terraced vineyards and dry-stone walls in the countryside of Pantelleria
image.credit: Luca Volpi, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Asinara
items.subtitle: Sardinia, off the north-west tip
items.desc: For a century a prison and quarantine island, now a national park with no private cars, white donkeys and empty beaches. Visit from Stintino or Porto Torres on a day trip, then explore by bike, electric car or guided tour. The old high-security prison is a sobering stop.
items.meta: Why: wild coast with a dark past · When: April to June, September

image.alt: White buildings of Cala d'Oliva above clear blue water on Asinara island
image.credit: Tomi, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Tremiti Islands
items.subtitle: Puglia, off the Gargano coast
items.desc: Puglia's only archipelago: pine-scented San Domino with its coves and sea caves, and San Nicola, crowned by a fortified medieval abbey. The water is a protected marine reserve and gloriously clear. Ferries and fast boats run from Termoli and the Gargano ports, mostly in summer.
items.meta: Why: Adriatic islands with Aegean water · When: June, September

image.alt: Boats moored in clear turquoise water off the white cliffs of the Tremiti Islands
image.credit: Carmen Fiano, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

sections.heading: Slow coasts
sections.intro: Seaside towns where the fishing boats are still working boats, and where the evening stroll matters more than the beach club.

items.title: Maratea
items.subtitle: Basilicata, Tyrrhenian coast
items.desc: Basilicata's only stretch of western coast: about 30 kilometres of cliffs, coves and black-sand beaches below a medieval hill town of many churches. A huge white statue of Christ the Redeemer stands on Monte San Biagio above it all. Intercity trains stop at Maratea station.
items.meta: Why: Amalfi-style cliffs without the crowds · When: June, September

image.alt: Green mountains dropping to the Tyrrhenian Sea along the coast of Maratea
image.credit: Benjamin Smith, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Scilla
items.subtitle: Calabria, Strait of Messina
items.desc: The rock of the sea monster in the Odyssey, now a castle above a fishing village. In the Chianalea quarter, houses rise straight out of the water and boats tie up at the front doors. In early summer, eat a swordfish sandwich made from the morning's catch.
items.meta: Why: myth, swordfish and water-lapped lanes · When: May to July

image.alt: Houses of the Chianalea quarter in Scilla rising straight from the clear sea
image.credit: Benjamin Smith, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Camogli
items.subtitle: Liguria, Riviera di Levante
items.desc: Tall painted houses crowd a pebble beach and a small harbour, just round the headland from glitzy Portofino. Walk or take the boat to the abbey of San Fruttuoso, eat focaccia on the sea wall, and time your visit for the giant-pan fish fry each May.
items.meta: Why: the Riviera at its most genuine · When: April to June, September to October

image.alt: The tall painted houses of Camogli lining its pebble beach
image.credit: Abldecn, CC BY 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Vieste
items.subtitle: Puglia, Gargano peninsula
items.desc: A white old town on a limestone promontory above long sandy beaches and the lonely sea stack of Pizzomunno. Take a boat to the sea caves, see the wooden trabucchi fishing machines along the coast, and drive inland into the deep beech woods of the Foresta Umbra.
items.meta: Why: beaches, caves and forest in one trip · When: June, September

image.alt: The white old town of Vieste on its promontory above the Adriatic
image.credit: Anczlu, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Cala Gonone
items.subtitle: Sardinia, Gulf of Orosei
items.desc: A small resort that is the gateway to the Gulf of Orosei, where limestone cliffs drop into impossibly blue water. Take a boat to Cala Luna or Cala Mariolu, explore the Bue Marino sea cave, or hike down to Cala Goloritzé, where visitor numbers are capped.
items.meta: Why: Sardinia's most dramatic coastline · When: late May to June, September

image.alt: Cala Gonone and the Gulf of Orosei below limestone mountains in Sardinia
image.credit: David Edgar, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

sections.heading: Mountain and lake hideaways
sections.intro: The quieter cousins of Como and Cortina, with better hiking, cheaper rooms and nights so dark you can see the Milky Way.

items.title: Lake Orta
items.subtitle: Piedmont, west of Lake Maggiore
items.desc: A small, romantic lake with one perfect village, Orta San Giulio, and an island monastery where signs along the single lane ask you to walk in silence. Climb the Sacro Monte, a UNESCO-listed path of frescoed chapels, and take the little boat across at sunset.
items.meta: Why: lake beauty at a whisper · When: April to June, September to October

image.alt: Lake Orta from above, with the island of San Giulio and Orta San Giulio on the far shore
image.credit: Hagai Agmon-Snir, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Val di Funes
items.subtitle: Trentino-Alto Adige, South Tyrol
items.desc: A farming valley below the sawtooth Odle (Geisler) peaks, home valley of the climber Reinhold Messner. The church of Santa Maddalena is famously photogenic; walk the Adolf Munkel trail beneath the peaks instead and stop at a mountain hut for dumplings and apple strudel.
items.meta: Why: the Dolomites at their most pastoral · When: June to October

image.alt: The village of Santa Maddalena in Val di Funes below the jagged Odle peaks in autumn
image.credit: Eric Kilby, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Val Grande
items.subtitle: Piedmont, above Lake Maggiore
items.desc: Italy's largest wilderness area, a national park of deep valleys and abandoned summer pastures that nature has reclaimed. There are no villages inside, just unstaffed huts and tough paths. For a gentler taste, walk from the edge villages above Verbania.
items.meta: Why: real wilderness near Milan · When: June to September

image.alt: Layered wooded ridges of the Val Grande wilderness with the Alps beyond
image.credit: Esponenziale, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Lago di Braies, off-season
items.subtitle: Trentino-Alto Adige, Dolomites
items.desc: This emerald lake under the cliffs of the Croda del Becco is mobbed in July and August, when car access works on a booking system. Come in late September or October for golden larches and an empty shoreline loop, or in deep winter, when the lake freezes and falls silent.
items.meta: Why: a postcard without the queue · When: late September to October, January to February

image.alt: Rowing boats on the emerald water of Lago di Braies below Dolomite cliffs
image.credit: kallerna, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Bagni di Lucca
items.subtitle: Tuscany, Serchio valley
items.desc: A faded spa town in wooded hills where Shelley, Byron and the Brownings came to take the waters. Cross the 19th-century chain bridge, soak in the thermal caves, and visit the humpbacked Devil's Bridge at nearby Borgo a Mozzano. Lucca is under an hour away by train.
items.meta: Why: Tuscany's green, overlooked side · When: May to October

image.alt: Old houses along the River Lima at Ponte a Serraglio in Bagni di Lucca
image.credit: H005, Public domain, via Wikimedia Commons

sections.heading: Cities without the crowds
sections.intro: Handsome, lively, well-fed cities that most itineraries skip. Each makes a better base than you would think.

items.title: Trieste
items.subtitle: Friuli Venezia Giulia, on the Slovenian border
items.desc: A Habsburg port city where Italian, Slovene and Austrian worlds meet. Piazza Unità d'Italia opens straight onto the sea, the old coffee houses are where James Joyce wrote, and locals sunbathe on the Barcola promenade. In season, seek out an osmiza, a Karst farmhouse selling its own wine.
items.meta: Why: coffee, sea air and Mitteleuropa · When: May to October

image.alt: Miramare Castle on its rocky promontory above the sea near Trieste
image.credit: Adiel lo, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Lecce
items.subtitle: Puglia, Salento
items.desc: A honey-coloured city of riotous Baroque carved from soft local limestone, with a Roman amphitheatre half-buried in its main square. Start the day with a warm pasticciotto custard pastry, browse the papier-mâché workshops, and use it as a base for the Salento beaches.
items.meta: Why: the Baroque capital of the south · When: April to June, September to October

image.alt: The Roman amphitheatre and St Orontius column in Piazza Sant'Oronzo, Lecce
image.credit: Benjamin Smith, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Mantua
items.subtitle: Lombardy, on three lakes
items.desc: The Gonzaga dukes' city, ringed by lakes formed from the River Mincio. Inside the vast Palazzo Ducale is Mantegna's painted Bridal Chamber; across town, Giulio Romano's Palazzo Te is pure Renaissance fun. Eat tortelli di zucca, pumpkin pasta with a hint of mostarda.
items.meta: Why: Renaissance art without the queues · When: April to June, September to October

image.alt: The long Renaissance facade and lawn of Palazzo Te in Mantua
image.credit: Marcok, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Urbino
items.subtitle: Marche, on a ridge in the Montefeltro hills
items.desc: Raphael's home town and the ideal Renaissance court, built around Duke Federico da Montefeltro's palace. Its National Gallery of the Marche holds Piero della Francesca's enigmatic Flagellation. The university keeps the steep brick streets young and the bars cheap.
items.meta: Why: a whole Renaissance city on a hill · When: April to June, September to October

image.alt: Aerial view of Urbino's old town and Ducal Palace on its ridge in the Montefeltro hills
image.credit: KAP Jasa, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Ascoli Piceno
items.subtitle: Marche, near the Abruzzo border
items.desc: A city built almost entirely of pale travertine, whose Piazza del Popolo is one of Italy's most beautiful squares. Order an anisette at Caffè Meletti, eat olive all'ascolana, crisp fried stuffed olives, and come in summer for the Quintana jousting tournament.
items.meta: Why: a travertine jewel box · When: May to October

image.alt: The arcaded travertine Piazza del Popolo in Ascoli Piceno under a blue sky
image.credit: Alessandro Bonvini, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Bergamo
items.subtitle: Lombardy, an hour from Milan
items.desc: Most people only see Bergamo's airport. Take the funicular up to the Città Alta instead: a medieval upper town wrapped in UNESCO-listed Venetian walls, with Piazza Vecchia at its heart. Stay for casoncelli, butter-and-sage stuffed pasta, and a walk along the ramparts at dusk.
items.meta: Why: a hilltop old town next to the airport · When: year-round

image.alt: Piazza Vecchia in Bergamo's Città Alta with the Contarini fountain and the civic tower
image.credit: Steffen Schmitz, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

items.title: Ferrara
items.subtitle: Emilia-Romagna, between Bologna and Venice
items.desc: The Este family's Renaissance city, planned with wide streets and centred on a moated castle. Locals go everywhere by bike, and so should you: the nine kilometres of city walls make a perfect green ring to ride. Try cappellacci di zucca with butter and sage.
items.meta: Why: Italy's best city by bike · When: April to October

image.alt: Cyclists and walkers in Piazza Trento e Trieste beside Ferrara Cathedral
image.credit: Ввласенко, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

tips: Stay at least one night in a village: the lanes empty by late afternoon and you will have them to yourself.
Many small islands and coastal towns run reduced ferries, and close hotels and restaurants, from November to March, so check timetables before you plan.
Rural Italy is much easier with a car; where we suggest a train or ferry instead, we have said so.
Look for the Borghi più Belli d'Italia and Bandiere Arancioni signs at village entrances: they are a reliable guide to well-kept places.
In August, Italians head to the coast and the mountains too. For quiet, aim for June or September.
